ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Enlarged prostate, or benign prostatic hyperplasia, is a common age‑related growth that can obstruct urine flow and cause retention. It is diagnosed clinically and confirmed with PSA, ultrasound, and sometimes biopsy. Management balances symptom relief, medication, and surgery.

sections.p: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non‑malignant proliferation of stromal and epithelial cells in the prostate, leading to urinary outflow obstruction. Diagnosis starts with history, digital rectal exam (DRE), PSA, and post‑void residual (PVR) measurement. Ultrasound or MRI confirms size and rule out cancer.
b: History of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)
DRE shows a smooth, enlarged gland

t.b: Is PSA elevated? A high PSA (>10 ng/mL) raises suspicion for prostate cancer and may prompt biopsy.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and prostate volume. Staging informs treatment choice.

t.b: What is the symptom burden? Higher scores mean more severe obstruction.

sections.p: The primary driver is age‑related hormonal changes, especially dihydrotestosterone (DHT) stimulating stromal growth. Other factors include genetics, metabolic syndrome, and chronic inflammation.

t.b: Is testosterone low? Low levels can worsen LUTS but are not a direct cause of BPH.
Elevated CRP or ESR may indicate prostatitis contributing to symptoms.

sections.p: Patients report hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia, incomplete emptying, and urinary retention. In low‑resource settings, symptoms may be mistaken for infection or bladder stones.

t.b: Does it show infection? A negative dipstick rules out UTI as the primary cause.
Is there bacterial growth? Positive culture indicates concurrent infection.

sections.p: Key tests assess obstruction, infection, and rule out cancer. In resource‑poor areas, simple tools like bedside ultrasound and PSA suffice.

t.b: Is PSA >10 ng/mL? Suggests possible cancer.
Is there bacterial growth? Treat infection first.
Is the prostate smooth and enlarged? Confirms BPH.

sections.p: Urgent signs include acute urinary retention, hematuria, fever, or rapidly worsening symptoms. Complications can be bladder stones, infection, or renal failure.

t.b: Do creatinine and BUN rise? Indicates renal impairment from obstruction.
Does it show hydronephrosis? Signals back‑pressure on kidneys.

faq.a: BPH is managed but not cured; treatment controls symptoms and prevents complications.
Surgery is reserved for severe or refractory cases; many patients respond to medication.
BPH itself is benign, but a high PSA may warrant biopsy to rule out cancer.

exam: Explain how DHT contributes to prostate enlargement and why 5‑α‑reductase inhibitors are effective.
Describe the diagnostic workup for a patient with suspected BPH in a low‑resource setting.
